h1: Wedding Guest Dresses Over 50: Age-Appropriate Elegance
intro: Wedding guest dresses over 50 are chosen the same way as anyone's, starting with the dress code, but the details that make a dress comfortable for a long day matter more: fabric that skims rather than clings, straps and sleeves that work with real underwear, and a hem you can sit, stand and dance in. There is no age at which a color, a hemline or bare arms become off-limits. The picks below favor midi sheaths, A-lines and wrap dresses, and the guide covers the fit points worth checking before you order.

contentSections.heading: Start with the dress code, not your age
contentSections.content:
The invitation sets the length and fabric, exactly as it does for every other guest. The Emily Post Institute's attire guide lists, for women: a floor-length evening gown, a dressy cocktail dress or your dressiest little black dress for black tie; a short afternoon or cocktail dress, a little black dress, a long dressy skirt and top, or dressy separates for semi-formal; a dress, a skirt and dressy top, or a dressy pants outfit for dressy casual.

That list is useful for two reasons. It shows that long skirts, dressy separates and pantsuits are on the list at most dress codes, so you never have to choose between a short dress and a gown. And it makes the midi the natural workhorse: it suits semi-formal, cocktail and dressy casual weddings, and a dressy midi passes at most formal daytime weddings too. Tea-length, which ends between the calf and the ankle, is a good alternative when you want more coverage than a midi without the hemming that a floor-length dress needs.

contentSections.heading: Fit points worth checking in the listing
contentSections.content:
These are the details that decide whether a dress is comfortable after the first hour.

Fabric weight and lining. A medium-weight crepe, a stretch crepe or a lined satin skims the body and holds its shape. Thin, unlined jersey and very light polyester cling and show every seam. If the listing does not mention a lining, assume there is none.

Bra-friendly straps and necklines. Look at the strap width and the back. Wider straps, cap sleeves and higher backs hide a regular bra; spaghetti straps and low backs need specialist underwear.

Arm openings. A close, high armhole lets you hug and dance without the dress riding up, and keeps the bra hidden from the side.

The zip. A side zip, or a back zip with a pull you can reach, saves a struggle when you are dressing alone.

Stretch. A small percentage of spandex in a fitted dress makes a long dinner far more comfortable.

Shoes. Choose the shoes with the dress. Kitten heels, block heels, low wedges and dressy flats look polished and let you stand through photographs and dance afterwards; a hem should be set to the shoe you will actually wear.

contentSections.heading: Sleeves and coverage, if you want them
contentSections.content:
Coverage is a preference, not a rule. Many women wear sleeveless and strapless dresses to weddings at every age; others prefer their arms covered. If you do want sleeves, the options differ more than they look in photos.

The comparison below sets out the trade-offs. In short: three-quarter sleeves are the most versatile, sheer sleeves give coverage without warmth, and a matching jacket gives you both options in one outfit. For more on sleeved and covered styles, see the long sleeve and modest wedding guest dress pages.

contentSections.heading: Color and print
contentSections.content:
Wear any color you feel good in. Rich jewel tones, such as emerald, sapphire and burgundy, photograph strongly and suit day or evening. Navy is an easy alternative to black. Dusty rose, berry and wine are warm without being loud. Bright coral, fuchsia and cobalt are just as appropriate as they are for any guest.

Two cautions apply to everyone, not to age. Avoid white, ivory and cream, and be careful with very pale champagne and silver, which can read white in photographs. And if you know the bridesmaids' color, choose a clearly different shade.

For prints, refined florals, geometrics and tone-on-tone patterns work well. If you prefer solids, a texture such as lace, beading or jacquard adds interest.

contentSections.heading: When you are close to the couple
contentSections.content:
Guests over 50 are often aunts, family friends or the parents of close friends, and some have been, or will be, a mother of the bride or groom themselves. As a guest you have more freedom than the wedding party: you are not coordinating with a palette or with the other mother, so choose what suits you.

It is still worth a quick check if you will be in many family photographs. Ask whether the couple has a color they would like guests to avoid, and steer away from the mothers' colors if you know them. If you attend several weddings a year, one well-cut dress in navy, emerald or deep rose with two or three changes of jacket, shoes and jewelry covers most of them. The site's mother of the bride page covers the role itself if you are dressing for it.

faqs.question: Are sleeveless dresses OK for women over 50?
faqs.answer: Yes. There is no etiquette rule about bare arms and age. If you prefer coverage, a three-quarter or flutter sleeve, a sheer sleeve, or a matching jacket or wrap all work. The only time coverage is a rule rather than a preference is at a religious venue that asks for it.

faqs.question: Can women over 50 wear bright colors to a wedding?
faqs.answer: Yes. Emerald, sapphire, ruby, coral, fuchsia and cobalt are all appropriate. The color rules that apply to every guest still apply: avoid white, ivory and cream, and avoid the bridesmaids' exact shade.

faqs.question: What is too revealing for a wedding guest over 50?
faqs.answer: The same things that are too revealing for any guest: very short hems, very low necklines and fully sheer fabric at most weddings, and bare shoulders at venues that ask for coverage. Beyond that, the dress code and the venue should guide you, not your birthday.

answer: Wedding guest dresses over 50 follow the invitation's dress code like anyone else's: a midi or tea-length dress for cocktail and semi-formal, a floor-length gown or dressy cocktail dress for black tie. What changes is the fit you look for: lined fabric with some weight, straps that cover a bra, sleeves or a matching jacket if you want coverage, and shoes you can stand in for hours.
